finding.claim: Missing await on authorize() in DELETE /reports/:id lets any caller, including anonymous callers, delete any report regardless of grants (BOLA / broken authorization). Critical.
finding.source: DELETE /reports/:id request from any caller; req.user may be undefined (server.js:5 copies req.session.user with no check)

trace.note: db.reports.get loads the report by req.params.id
authorize(req.user,'delete',report) called without await; returns a promise that is never observed
authorize body: db.grants lookup and grants.includes check; throws 403 (or TypeError when req.user is undefined) inside the discarded promise
remove executes regardless of authorization outcome

finding.guards_checked: server.js:4-7 only copies session user onto req.user, enforces nothing; no auth-required gate on any route; no error middleware; PUT handler at server.js:27 correctly awaits authorize, so the bug is specific to DELETE; express.json at server.js:3 is irrelevant to this path

verdict.guard_found: No effective authorization guard. The only relevant control is server.js:5, which dereferences req.session.user; the directory contains only server.js and no session middleware is defined or required in it, so req.session is undefined and line 5 throws a TypeError before the DELETE handler runs, which would return a 500. That is a deployment artifact, not an authorization check.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: authorize() at server.js:20 is called without await, so db.reports.remove at server.js:21 runs before the grant check at server.js:10-15 can throw, and the PUT handler at server.js:27 does await. Whether an anonymous caller can reach that handler depends on session middleware (req.session at server.js:5) that is not in the provided code, so reachability cannot be decided from the code available, though if an upstream session layer sets req.session with no user, the deletion does occur.

finding.claim: Discarded authorize() rejections (DELETE line 20) and un-caught 403 throws from the async PUT handler (line 27) become unhandled promise rejections, which crash the Node process under Node 15+ default settings. Conditional on Express 4 and Node 15+. High (DoS).
finding.source: Any DELETE by a user without delete grant, any PUT by a user without write grant, or any anonymous PUT/DELETE (req.user undefined)
finding.sink: Unhandled promise rejection -> process exit (--unhandled-rejections=throw default)

trace.note: authorize throws err with status 403 (or TypeError on undefined user)
DELETE: promise not awaited, rejection unhandled
PUT: await rethrows inside async route handler; Express 4 does not forward async rejections to error middleware
single process hosts all routes, so exit takes down the service

finding.guards_checked: No process.on('unhandledRejection') handler, no try/catch or .catch in the file, no error-handling middleware; err.status=403 at server.js:13 is only honoured by Express 5 or an explicit error handler, neither present. Express and Node versions unknown (no package.json in directory), so this is conditional.

verdict.guard_found: none. server.js has no process-level unhandledRejection handler, no try/catch or .catch around the handlers, and no error middleware. The only error-related code is the err.status=403 throw at server.js:13-14, which nothing catches. The authorize() call at server.js:20 is a bare statement with no await, so its rejection is discarded. The authorize() call at server.js:27 is awaited inside an async handler with no catch. Nothing in the file blocks an anonymous or low-privilege caller from reaching these paths.
verdict.reason: server.js:20 calls the async authorize() without await or .catch, so any DELETE by a user lacking the delete grant (or with req.user undefined, which makes db.grants throw a TypeError at server.js:10) produces an unhandled rejection, and Node 15+ defaults to exiting the process on that; no handler exists anywhere in server.js, so the DELETE path crashes independent of Express version, while the PUT path at server.js:27 additionally depends on Express 4 not forwarding async rejections, as the candidate states.

finding.claim: A request referencing a nonexistent report ID causes an unhandled TypeError (report.id / resource.id on a null report) that crashes the process under the same Express 4 / Node 15+ conditions. Medium (DoS), requires no credentials.
finding.source: DELETE or PUT to /reports/:id with an ID that does not exist, from anonymous or authenticated caller
finding.sink: Unhandled rejection from report.id access -> process exit

trace.note: db.reports.get returns null/undefined for unknown ID (assumed; db layer not in repo)
DELETE: authorize reads resource.id on null report inside un-awaited promise (unhandled)
DELETE: report.id throws TypeError in async handler
PUT: same null report flows into authorize at line 27

finding.guards_checked: No null check on report and no 404 response path in either handler; no error middleware. Behaviour depends on db.reports.get returning a falsy value rather than throwing, which could not be verified.

verdict.guard_found: none. There is no null check or 404 path in the DELETE (server.js:18-23) or PUT (server.js:25-30) handlers, no try/catch, and no error middleware. The error middleware at server.js:4-7 only sets req.user. authorize (server.js:9-16) throws on a missing grant but fails earlier on the null resource (resource.id at line 10), and the DELETE call at line 20 discards its promise.
verdict.reason: For an unknown ID, db.reports.get (server.js:19/26) yields a falsy report or throws, and either way the async handler rejects (server.js:21 report.id, or server.js:27 via authorize's resource.id at line 10); Express 4 does not catch async rejections, so Node 15+ crashes on the unhandled rejection. The attacker can be anonymous, because with express-session req.user is undefined and user.id at line 10 throws the same way. Caveat: the session middleware and db layer are not in the repo, so reachability depends on that deployment assumption; the trace itself matches the code. The same unawaited authorize at server.js:20 also means a valid but forbidden DELETE crashes the process, which is a broader version of this finding.

finding.claim: PUT /reports/:id passes the full unfiltered request body to db.reports.update, enabling mass assignment of any report field the client sends, including potentially privileged fields such as owner, tenant or ACL attributes. Medium, unverified.
finding.source: req.body (JSON parsed by express.json at server.js:3) from any caller holding write grant on the report

trace.note: express.json parses arbitrary JSON body into req.body
await authorize(req.user,'write',report) passes for write-capable caller
entire req.body persisted via db.reports.update with no field allow-list

finding.guards_checked: No field allow-list or schema validation in server.js; authorization checks only the write action, not which fields are written; report schema and db.reports.update implementation are outside this repo, so whether privileged fields or id can actually be overwritten is unconfirmed.

verdict.guard_found: server.js:27 `await authorize(req.user, "write", report)` is a real guard. It throws a 403 on failure (server.js:9-16), and the throw is not caught, so it blocks non-write callers. It only checks the action, not which fields are written. No field allow-list or schema validation exists in server.js (server.js:28 passes req.body unfiltered).
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: express.json populates req.body (server.js:3), a write-granted caller passes authorize (server.js:27), and the whole body reaches db.reports.update (server.js:28). Whether that reaches privileged fields like owner or ACL cannot be decided, because the report schema and db.reports.update live outside this repo, so the claimed escalation is unconfirmed.
